item.content:encoded:
Running back Trevor Etienne is on his way back to the Panthers lineup.

The team announced that Etienne has been designated to return from injured reserve. Etienne hurt his ankle in August and became eligible to return to action after Carolina beat the Lions in Week 4, but his 2026 debut had to wait for the team to return from their bye week.

Etienne was a 2025 fourth-round pick and he served as a returner in addition to seeing limited action on offense during his rookie season. Chuba Hubbard and AJ Dillon are the current running backs on the team's 53-man roster.

The Panthers also announced that they have placed defensive tackle Cam Jackson on injured reserve. Jackson has a shoulder injury.

The Jackson move leaves the Panthers with three open slots on their active roster. They've also designated offensive tackle Taylor Moton and defensive lineman Turk Wharton for return this week, so all three could be back for their Week 6 game against the Eagles.

item.title: Christian Parker seems to be getting Sean Desai’d by the Cowboys
item.description: Things aren’t going so well for the former Eagles assistant coach down in Dallas.
item.content:encoded:
You may have noticed that former Philadelphia Eagles passing game coordinator/defensive backs coach Christian Parker is off to a rough start as the Dallas Cowboys’ defensive coordinator.

Here’s how the Cowboys’ defense ranks in a number of metrics exiting Week 5:

  • 31st in yards allowed per game (395.4)
  • 26th in offensive points allowed per game (27.2)
  • 32nd in EPA per play
  • 32nd in success rate

Yikes.

Given these struggles, the Cowboys are reportedly hiring a more experienced assistant to pair with Parker as a first-time play-caller: Mike Pettine.

And not only are they bringing the Bucks County, Pennsylvania native into the fold. But the Cowboys are also moving Parker from his normal role on the sideline to the booth.

It’s hard to look at this setup and not think back to when the Eagles bizarrely decided to put Matt Patricia in charge of their defense mid-stream during the 2023 season, effectively demoting Sean Desai in the process without actually formally doing so.

That setup ended up being an abject disaster for the Eagles, who historically collapsed at the end of that season.

Maybe this approach will go better for the Cowboys given that Parker and Pettine actually have experience working together. Ed Werder offered some more insight on this move:

The Cowboys are carefully representing the hiring of Pettine as someone who is here to support Christian Parker and offer advice based on his experience. But NFL coaches I’ve spoken to who know Pettine and the dynamics of the situation with the Cowboys believe the more influence and responsibility Pettine has, the better for the team.

One HC who had Pettine on his staff: “They finally hired a real coach. Pettine is legit. Dallas will walk away with that division now.”

But maybe not and we can all laugh at the Cowboys for being such a mess.

If Parker does eventually end up getting canned by the Cowboys, which is the fate that Desai met after the 2023 season, it’ll be interesting to see what’s next for him. He had a lot of success in Philly as an assistant coach, which is what landed him his current job. There was some thought the Eagles viewed him as a potential Vic Fangio successor. But that may no longer be the case.

Something to monitor!

item.title: Suspension likely for Rams tackle Alaric Jackson for punching Bills' Bradley Chubb after loss
item.description: A suspension appears likely after Rams star left tackle Alaric Jackson punched Bills linebacker Bradley Chubb after the Rams' overtime 'MNF' loss at SoFi Stadium.
item.content:encoded:
Alaric Jackson has a history of violent outbursts. Still, it was surprising to see the Rams star offensive tackle punch Buffalo Bills linebacker Bradley Chubb on the SoFi Stadium field moments after the Bills defeated the Rams 37-34 in overtime on Monday.

Players were milling around midfield, exchanging jerseys and making small talk when Chubb appeared to say something to Jackson, who was chatting with another Bills player. Jackson immediately marched over to Chubb and slugged him once in the face, knocking a cap from his head.

Players from both teams intervened, and the episode was documented on video by the NFL. Based on precedent, Jackson, 28, likely faces a suspension.

One year ago, Detroit Lions safety Brian Branch was suspended for one game after he smacked Kansas City Chiefs receiver JuJu Smith-Schuster in the helmet after a game.

At the time, Branch spoke to reporters in the locker room and admitted his actions were “childish.”

Jackson did not make himself available for an interview after Monday’s incident, although Chubb did.

“It’s just emotions, you know what I mean? Emotional game. It was a close game,” Chubb said. “And, you know, they always catch the second guy. So, I let him swing. And then my teammates held me back, and I just chilled.”

Read more:Rams’ special teams woes leave Sean McVay 'sick' after frustrating overtime loss to Bills

Jackson averted a suspension ahead of this season when authorities declined to file formal criminal charges after he was arrested on suspicion of felony domestic violence. Police responded to a call at a home in West Hills on June 8 at 11 p.m. and said in a report that the 6-foot-7, 338-pound Jackson was arrested for “willfully inflicting physical or corporal injury resulting in a ‘traumatic condition’ [such as a bruise, scratch, swelling, or internal injury] on an intimate partner.”

Jackson, who is in his sixth season with the Rams and fourth as quarterback Matthew Stafford’s blindside protector, entered a diversion program that required him to complete probation and anger management classes. Four months earlier, he had signed a three-year contract that included $35 million in guarantees. He is scheduled to earn $18.4 million this season.

In 2024, Jackson was suspended for two games by the NFL for violating its personal conduct policy following a lawsuit filed by a woman alleging he recorded her without her consent during sex. The woman, who also reported it to the league, alleged that Jackson refused to delete the video and taunted her with it. The civil suit was dismissed.

item.title: The Rams are down, but not out
item.description: Things aren’t good for Sean McVay and Co., but there’s a path forward.
item.content:encoded:
There’s no question that Sean McVay and the Rams would take a few do-overs this season. From traveling to Australia to play on no rest, losing to the Broncos in a game they should have won, and topping it off on Monday Night Football by letting a potential comeback win slip through their fingers. Los Angeles finds itself at 2-3 on the season, locked in third place in the NFC West, and looking up at the 49ers who are 5-0, looking like the juggernaut of the division.

The situation may look really bad, especially for a team that was universally hailed as a Super Bowl contender, but the full picture really isn’t that bad for the Rams — at least not yet.

While the 2-3 record is bad in isolation, we have seen significant improvement from the Rams over the last two weeks. Matthew Stafford looks more comfortable under center after a rocky start, Puka Nacua is back in the lineup after being injured, and the team is positioned to get even better with Myles Garrett (hopefully) returning by Week 9.

Even if Garrett isn’t able to return on his earliest timeline, the next five weeks are extremely beneficial for the Rams:

  • vs. Cardinals
  • @ Raiders
  • vs. Chargers
  • @ Commanders
  • @ Cardinals

Facing teams with a combined record of 6-18-1, the only team that appears remotely poised to challenge is the Raiders — who could be in the midst of pivoting their season to getting Fernando Mendoza reps, over trying to compete with Kirk Cousins. There is a very real chance we see this Rams team enter their Week 10 bye at 7-3, back in the mix in the division, and the frontrunner for a Wild Card spot in the NFC.

That doesn’t mean the Rams are without problems, however. Matthew Stafford has been very scattershot across five games. His accuracy has slipped, despite having a shallower Average Depth of Target (ADoT). This means he’s struggling more, despite making easier throws. More importantly, throwing six interceptions in five games is wild, considering he threw just eight in 17 games last season. There’s little margin for error defensively without Garrett in the lineup, and that’s being exploited.

The run defense in particular has been extremely suspect across five games. The Rams are currently giving up 4.6 yards-per-carry, good for 24th in the NFL and sit middle of the league in plays allowed per drive, largely because teams have been able to consistently run the ball well. This has compounded to result in Los Angeles giving up 24.0 points per game, which ranks 20th in the NFL — and scoring 23.8 per game on average.

The Rams are by no means “done,” but they have a lot to fix. Monday Night Football was indicative of this. The Bills are one of the best teams in the league, but the Rams had a reputation entering 2026 that they would be an all-consuming force that even the best teams would struggle against. That simply hasn’t been the case, and even after making big trades to shore up both their defensive line and secondary, still we have a team that is failing to reach its true potential.

This is what makes the 2026 version of the Rams so fascinating. Routinely a team seen as “in the mix,” the roster has always been elevated because of Sean McVay and his coaching staff. There would be glaring holes on both sides of the ball, yet McVay and Co. would always have a plan, a way to scheme around it, and ultimately produce a team that felt like a Super Bowl contender. This year, it just doesn’t feel like that. There’s a swagger and a vibe that’s lacking, yet this is when we’d assume the Rams would be at the most confident with Trent McDuffie in the secondary and all their weapons back.

One thing is abundantly clear: The return of Myles Garrett can’t come quickly enough. This team needs an injection of energy on the defensive side of the ball in the worst way possible. If that happens in or around the bye week, and the Rams can get back on track — watch out. If not, well, this could be one of the most staggering failures a team has had in recent years.

item.title: Extreme “Special Teams” Makeover: Rams edition
item.description: The Rams need to make a move on special teams, is Matt Gay the answer?
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Rams are -31.8 in Special Teams EPA through five weeks, making their third phase a catastrophic liability that threatens to undermine an otherwise competitive football team. If Sean McVay and Les Snead want to maximize this roster’s Super Bowl potential, an extreme special teams makeover needs to be on the table, starting with a reliable kicker who can consistently turn scoring opportunities into points. The Rams have two outside options worth considering if they want to fix their special teams problems before they cost them another game: trading for a familiar face or signing one of the most accurate kickers in NFL history.

Option 1: Trade for Matt Gay

A reunion with Matt Gay could be exactly what the Rams need to stabilize their kicking game. Gay is currently with the Las Vegas Raiders on a one-year contract that expires after the 2026 season, making him a potential trade target if the Raiders are willing to negotiate.

Gay already knows what it takes to succeed in Los Angeles. During his two-and-a-half seasons with the Rams from 2020 through 2022, he converted 74 of 80 field goal attempts, good for an impressive 92.5% success rate. His best season came in 2021, when he made 94.1% of his field goals and helped the Rams capture Super Bowl LVI.

Although Gay’s career field goal percentage sits at approximately 84.6%, his previous success in Los Angeles gives the Rams reason to believe he could rediscover his best form. He has also demonstrated the ability to make long kicks, including a 59-yarder for Las Vegas in 2026.

A trade would give the Rams a proven option who understands the organization and has experience performing under championship expectations. With Gay’s contract expiring after this season, Los Angeles could potentially acquire him without committing to a long-term deal.

Option 2: Sign Justin Tucker

If the Rams prefer to pursue a different route, Justin Tucker represents another intriguing possibility. Tucker has a career field goal percentage of 89.1%, making him one of the most accurate kickers the NFL has seen. From 49 yards or less, his 94.8% success rate is nearly automatic.

The biggest question is whether Tucker can return to his previous level of consistency. His track record is difficult to ignore, but the Rams would need to evaluate his current form and availability before making a commitment. If he can still deliver that kind of accuracy, he would give Los Angeles a dependable option whenever the offense stalls outside the red zone.

Verdict: Either

The Rams cannot afford to keep surrendering valuable points and field position because of special teams mistakes. Trading for Gay offers familiarity, proven success in Los Angeles and a relatively short contractual commitment. Tucker provides a potentially high-upside alternative if the Rams believe he can recapture his elite form.

Either move would represent a meaningful step toward fixing a unit that has become a glaring weakness. With championship aspirations, the Rams need to stop treating special teams as an afterthought and start investing in solutions. An extreme makeover might be exactly what this team needs to turn a major liability into a legitimate strength.

item.title: Cowboys will give the Packers defense its biggest test yet
item.description: The Cowboys passing game is much better than what Green Bay has faced to this point.
item.content:encoded:
Coming out of week five, the Green Bay Packers’ defense has been a pleasant surprise on the season. Without Micah Parsons for a single snap yet, they rank eighth in EPA allowed per dropback and they rank an outstanding third in ANY/A value, as seen below from Justis Mosqueda.

Under the hood, though, things look shakier. Firstly, the Packers are tied with the Seattle Seahawks for the league lead in interceptions. Turnovers are notoriously noisy, and often a product of who you have played against, most notably which quarterbacks you have faced, and that is a lot of the story for Green Bay thus far. In week one, the Packers mostly faced Carson Wentz, the Vikings’ backup quarterback. In weeks two and three, the Packers faced Geno Smith and Michael Penix Jr, both starters, but then faced an undrafted rookie backup in week four and then both a second and third string quarterback in week five.

So while the numbers look promising early on, the grain of salt they should be taken with is larger than a boulder. In success rate, the cracks are already there. While Green Bay is eighth in EPA allowed per dropback, they are 17th in success rate allowed through the air. Again, this is against mostly backup quarterbacks and a Jets passing game that ranks 20th in EPA-per-dropback and 19th in dropback success rate. By DVOA, which doesn’t know that a backup quarterback played in a specific game but only takes the season-long performance of a unit, the Packers defense has played the fifth easiest schedule in the NFL thus far. The gap between Green Bay and the top three is relatively small, about as large as the gap between Green Bay and eighth, and much of that can be made up when taking into account they faced two full games of snaps of Jalon Daniels, Tyson Bagent, and Case Keenum rather than Baker Mayfield and Caleb Williams. And that’s before getting into whatever perceived differences you have between Carson Wentz and Kyler Murray.

This week, Green Bay will have no such luck. While the Dallas defense is a travesty, their offense can still hum. Their passing game ranks fifth in passing DVOA and fourth in EPA-per-dropback. Their two wide receivers could present significant problems for the Packers. The Packers do not have the typical archetype to match up with George Pickens’ size, and the struggles at cornerback with tackling could present significant problems with CeeDee Lamb’s YAC ability. Former Wisconsin Badger Jake Ferguson also presents a matchup problem for Green Bay’s linebackers, with both Zaire Franklin and Isaiah McDuffie being stumpier thumping linebackers, so expect to see just as much if not more Ty’Ron Hopper than we did against Chicago.

The challenge gets no easier going forward, as Green Bay will face Dak Prescott, Jared Goff, Drake Maye, and Matthew Stafford all before December, with Micah Parsons maybe back for the matchups with Maye and Stafford in November. As the offense is finally clicking the past two weeks (drops against Tampa aside), whether or not the defense can continue to produce, forcing more punts as the turnovers inevitably subside and the opposing quarterback schedule improves, will decide if the Packers can keep themselves on track to a playoff spot. They don’t need the defense to be great, particularly without Micah Parsons, but they need it to be just good enough to let the passing offense win them games.

The Packers will see across the field on Sunday a team that has run into the problem of what happens when the defense falls apart with that exact formula. They need to avoid a similar fate.

item.title: Fantasy Football Week 6 Backup RB Rankings: Kimani Vidal joins party to make Chargers' backfield more frustrating
item.description: Fred Zinkie takes you through his rankings of the top backup RBs going into Week 6 for fantasy football.
item.content:encoded:
Let's take a look at the backup RBs, who are listed in the order that they should be rostered, taking into account both their immediate fantasy football value as a flex option and their long-term potential to take on a larger role. Current roster rates are listed in parentheses.

1. Braelon Allen, Jets (84% rostered on Yahoo)

Allen is back in this space after a one-week hiatus, as the return of Breece Hall from a quad injury would demote him to backup status. Allen certainly proved his value to the team over the past two weeks, especially when he gained 116 yards on 24 carries in a rainy Week 5 win over the Browns.

In the absence of Hall, Allen has handled a heavier snap share and workload than anyone could have imagined. His usage suggests that he could have a role when Hall returns, which would be enough to keep Allen on fantasy rosters as we move through bye weeks. There is also a significant chance that Hall is unable to return in Week 6, which will keep Allen in the active lineup in most leagues.

2. Woody Marks, Texans (54%)

David Montgomery endured a disastrous Week 5, which included just 11 yards on five carries and a groin injury that will cause him to miss time. Marks took advantage of the additional opportunities, gaining 62 yards on 15 carries and 23 yards on four catches as the Texans routed the 0-5 Titans.

Marks has taken over the team lead in rushing yards, and although his 3.5 yards per carry is an unimpressive mark, it's still better than Montgomery's mark of 2.7. The second-year pro remains available in nearly half of Yahoo leagues, which could make him a Week 6 savior for those who must deal with a bye week for Jahmyr Gibbs, Chase Brown or Aaron Jones Sr. Some successful performances from Marks could permanently push him ahead of Montgomery on the depth chart. The one reason for skepticism is that Marks is set to face a Jaguars defense that has not allowed a running back to produce 40 rushing yards to this point in the season.

3. Kyle Monangai, Bears (85%)

Monangai missed Week 5 with thumb and toe injuries, and his status for Week 6 is unclear. His absence gave D'Andre Swift, who was benched after a Week 4 fumble, a chance to reassert himself as the team's top rusher. Swift did all he could in a lopsided loss to the Packers, gaining 73 total yards on nine carries with a TD and four catches.

The Bears desperately need Caleb Williams back, but they could also use the return of Monangai's physical running style. The second-year pro will have a significant role when he returns, which makes him worthy of a spot on fantasy benches.

4. Kimani Vidal, Chargers (3%)

The winless Chargers are arguably the most disappointing team in football, and their underachieving offense is the biggest reason. Vidal, who has spent the season ranked third on the team's depth chart, produced the only big play of Week 5, when he logged a 42-yard touchdown late in the third quarter. Vidal wound up recording 28 snaps to 23 for Keaton Mitchell and 20 for starter Omarion Hampton. Unfortunately, Vidal did little (15 yards) with his other seven carries.

The Chargers offense is a mess, partly due to an injury-ravaged offensive line. But with Hampton averaging 3.7 yards per carry, there is an opportunity for Vidal to take over rushing duties. After all, offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel's job likely hinges on finding a way to get this offense going next week in Kansas City.

5. Tyjae Spears, Titans (22%)

Tony Pollard continues to have a firm grip on the RB1 role in Tennessee after he gained 52 yards on 14 carries in Week 5, while Spears tallied zero yards on two carries. Spears managed to help those in PPR leagues by catching nine passes, but he turned that into just 28 yards.

Spears is on this list for one reason – Pollard is the most obvious trade candidate at the RB position. The 0-5 Titans can already give up on 2026, and the 29-year-old Pollard could help several competitive teams who are struggling with backfield injuries. If Pollard is traded prior to the Nov. 10 deadline, Spears will ascend to the top of the Titans depth chart and will warrant a roster spot in all fantasy leagues. Managers who have bench space can stash him now.

6. RJ Harvey, Broncos (84%)

Fantasy managers were looking forward to Week 5, as Sean Payton was set to take over play-calling duties for a sluggish Broncos offense. Unfortunately, not only did the group continue to underachieve, but Harvey had his worst game of the season. After catching 10 passes in Week 4, the second-year pro didn't record a catch and produced just seven yards on three carries. Starter J.K. Dobbins logged 18 carries and caught the ball twice.

If there is a silver lining for Harvey, it's that his 41% snap share wasn't dramatically different from Dobbins' 58% mark. That stat alone will keep him on this list, and on fantasy benches, while we hope that he earns more touches in Week 6. After all, Harvey still leads the Broncos with 20 catches.

7. Blake Corum, Rams (77%)

There were plenty of positives for Corum on Monday Night Football, especially given that his role in the Rams offense seemed to be in decline in the previous two weeks. He averaged 3.8 yards on five carries, which was better than Kyren Williams' 3.1 mark on his 16 rushes. Corum also gained 53 yards on three catches and found the end zone on a one-yard plunge in the third quarter. The bad news is that his snap share (27%) continued to lag far behind that of Williams (73%), and Corum didn't touch the ball in the fourth quarter or overtime.

Fantasy managers who drafted Corum in hopes of an even backfield split continue to be disappointed. But the third-year pro could have his best game of 2026 this week, as the Rams are bordering on two-touchdown favorites against the Cardinals. An early lead could result in Williams sitting out most of the second half.

8. Keaton Mitchell, Chargers (42%)

Having two Los Angeles RBs ranked among the top-10 backups at the position is a testament to the unsettled nature of the Chargers offense. While the snap shares and rushing totals of Hampton and Vidal continue to fluctuate, Mitchell has kept a steady role in the offense as a part-time rusher and the leading receiving option out of the backfield. The speedster did little on the ground in Week 5 (6 carries, 11 yards) but helped those in PPR leagues with 18 yards on three catches.

Managers who want to roll the dice on a possible impact RB should target the likes of Spears or Vidal. Mitchell's value is as a high-floor RB2 for those who are dealing with injuries or bye weeks. After all, he ranks second on the Chargers in catches and should continue to provide 5-10 points per week in PPR formats.

9. Samaje Perine, Bengals (3%)

Week 5 was supposed to be a "get right" game for Chase Brown, who has struggled on the ground all season. But even in a favorable matchup against the lowly Dolphins, Brown gained just 39 yards on 13 carries, with a long run of seven yards. Perine was much more effective, averaging 4.9 yards on his 14 carries, while also scoring a touchdown on one of his two catches.

The Bengals head into a Week 6 bye with Brown averaging 3.5 yards per carry. His long run this season is just 13 yards. Perine likely isn't any better than Brown, but the team needs to try something as they search for a respectable running game to complement the passing exploits of Joe Burrow. Don't be surprised if Perine has a significant role when the Bengals return to action in Week 7. If that happens, Perine will be a useful bye-week replacement in Week 8, when the Bengals enjoy a favorable home matchup against the Titans.

10. Brian Robinson, Falcons (49%)

The fact that Robinson grabbed the last spot on this list is a surefire sign that Week 5 wasn't a great one for backup running backs. The veteran is a clear backup to superstar Bijan Robinson, but on a Falcons team that relies heavily on the running game, that role has been good enough to rank him 31st in the NFL in rushing yards and tied for eighth in touchdowns.

Brian's greatest appeal is to serve as insurance for Bijan managers. But with the heaviest bye weeks on the horizon, he could be a low-end RB2 during weeks where the Falcons are expected to score plenty of points. Managers in deep formats can consider him for a home contest against the Bears this week.

item.title: Patriots injury analysis: Bad luck continues in Week 5
item.description: Analyzing the Patriots’ injury situation before their upcoming game against the Jets.
item.content:encoded:
The New England Patriots have plenty to feel good about coming out of their win over the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday. Their offense had its best day of the season, quarterback Drake Maye returned to his MVP form, and the defense had Kirk Cousins and the Raiders offense in a blender throughout the day.

However, the Patriots did not have perfect day either. Once again, after all, the injury bug bit them pretty hard.

With that said, here is our weekly injury analysis after rewatching the game.

Patriots injury analysis: NFL Week 5

RB TreVeyon Henderson: On the very next snap after catching a lateral from teammate Efton Chism in the second quarter, Henderson was tackled from behind on an 11-yard jet sweep. In the process, he suffered an ankle injury that forced him to leave the game and gingerly walk to the locker room. The second-year running back was originally announced as questionable to return and ultimately ruled out.

LT Will Campbell: Just two players after losing Henderson, the Patriots also saw Will Campbell go down. The starting left tackle was rolled up on from behind on a short run, staying down and grabbing his right knee — the same one he hurt last season when he tore his MCL and had to be placed on temporary injured reserve. He exited for the blue medical tent and later the locker room, but reappeared later in the second quarter. Campbell spent time on the sideline and riding a stationary bike. Despite the positive signs, however, he never returned to the game and did not reemerge after halftime.

CB Charles Woods: The Patriots were already down four cornerbacks entering Sunday, and another one got banged up midway through the third quarter. Charles Woods, who had started the game with Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis both absent, remained down on one knee after a tackle for loss. He was labeled as questionable to return with a shoulder injury — he already dealt with a shoulder issue coming into the game — but did eventually make his way back onto the field.

ED Dre’Mont Jones: Jones stayed down after rushing the passer in the fourth quarter. He did not appear to have absorbed any non-standard form of contact, but nonetheless required medical assistance on the field. He eventually got up and walked off the field into the blue medical tent, fist-bumping teammates along the way. The Patriots announced him as questionable to return with a shoulder injury and he was kept out for the remainder of the game.

DT Cory Durden: Durden had his feet tangled up after Raiders running back Dylan Laube’s touchdown in the fourth quarter, but he managed to walk to the bench under his own power. He did miss the ensuing extra point kick, but was back on the field at the next possibility thereafter: blocking on Andy Borregales’ point-after try to cap the Patriots’ next offensive possession.

What this means for the Patriots

Out of the five Patriots to get banged up on Sunday, three are question marks heading into Week 6: Will Campbell, TreVeyon Henderson, and Dre’Mont Jones.

Let’s start with Henderson, whose status was updated on Tuesday morning: he reportedly suffered a high ankle sprain that will keep him out for “multiple weeks” even though the Patriots are optimistic about a reasonably quick return. Still, Henderson being out will put pressure on a New England skill position group already without wideouts A.J. Brown and Mack Hollins. Rhamondre Stevenson and Corey Kiner are the top two running backs with Henderson out, with Lan Larison providing extra depth on the practice squad.

As for Campbell and Jones, they are in the TBD category for now. Jones’ injury didn’t appear overly serious when it happened, but that also does not mean his return to the field this week is guaranteed, particularly as far as full capacity is concerned. If he is limited our out versus the New York Jets, Elijah Ponder and Gabe Jacas will likely see an uptick of snaps again.

Campbell, meanwhile, is also expected to miss time after spraining his knee. First-round rookie Caleb Lomu took over and is set to continue lining up at left tackle until the nominal starter is cleared to return. When that happens remains to be seen, especially considering that Mike Vrabel sounded somewhat optimistic when talking about the second-year man on Monday.

Beyond the losses, the Patriots also might be getting some talent back soon: A.J. Brown, who suffered his own high ankle sprain in Week 1 and was subsequently placed on injured reserve, is eligible to return to practice this week. All signs point toward such a return happening sooner rather than later.

The Patriots will be back on the practice fields on Wednesday, starting their on-field preparation for the upcoming game against the Jets.

item.title: NFL reverses course, says Zxavian Harris is eligible to sign with team after trying to play for LSU
item.description: Zxavian Harris was ultimately left off LSU's roster after trying to return to college.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL is shifting gears on defensive tackle Zxavian Harris. After initially ruling Harris would not be eligible to sign with a professional team this season, the NFL reversed course Monday, telling teams Harris is an eligible free agent.

The league reportedly sent a memo to all 32 teams announcing that news, per NFL Network.

The NFL sent this memo to clubs regarding the decision to reinstate Zxavian Harris’ eligibility for the 2026 NFL season. pic.twitter.com/4yeVT1Focn

— Tom Pelissero (@TomPelissero) October 12, 2026

Harris and tight end Dae'Quan Wright found themselves the subject of controversy in September, when both men attempted to join Lane Kiffin at LSU despite spending time with NFL teams over the summer.

After going undrafted in the 2026 NFL Draft, Harris signed a deal with the New Orleans Saints. He was waived by the team in August, however. Wright spent time with the Philadelphia Eagles and Cleveland Browns before he was waived in late August.

With their NFL futures in jeopardy, Harris and Wright decided to see if they were eligible for a fifth year of college so they could play for LSU. That kicked off multiple contentious back-and-forths between Harris, Wright, LSU, the SEC and the NCAA.

In the end, LSU decided it wasn't worth risking the ire of the SEC and left both Harris and Wright off its roster.

The NFL then issued its initial ruling on both players, deeming them ineligible to sign with NFL teams in 2026 after attempting to return to college football.

Harris, however, had that decision reversed Monday after the NFL determined he did not participate in a single practice or game with LSU. Because of that, the league decided to make Harris an eligible free agent. Wright was not mentioned in the league's memo and remains ineligible to sign with an NFL team.

Now that he's eligible, it's unclear whether Harris will be signed by any team. Prior to his attempt to return to college, Harris was clearly on teams' radars, but was not good enough to make a final 53-man roster. Because of that, it's possible Harris draws attention as a possible practice squad player.

item.title: Cowboys DC Christian Parker moving from sideline to coaches' booth, says Jerry Jones
item.description: The Cowboys' defense is 31st in the NFL in yards allowed per game.
item.content:encoded:
Dallas Cowboys defensive coordinator Christian Parker is set to be moved from the sidelines to the coaches' booth for the rest of the season, owner and general manager Jerry Jones told 105.3 The Fan on Tuesday.

"You search for what we can do differently that would give us better results," Jones saidon his 84th birthday. "That's the main emphasis that we would spend some, let's say, specific attention to areas. We're going to coach the defense from not on the field, but up above. Parker's going up above.

"You should be looking for ways to adjust and make changes to improve. That's the point of improving from the results we had the last few weeks."

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Basketball league for the 2026-27 NBA season

The Cowboys dropped to 2-3 on the season following Thursday's loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Parker, who was hired in January, has already seen criticism directed his way from the likes of Wink Martindale and Mike Tomlin. Through five weeks the Dallas defense is 31st in the NFL with 395.4 yards allowed per game and has allowed a league-worst 168.4 rushing yards per game.

Thursday's defeat also marked the 12th straight game dating back to last season that Dallas has allowed at least 20 points.

Parker has held himself accountable publicly for the defense's lapses, but in an attempt to provide further assistance the Cowboys are bringing in longtime NFL defensive coordinator Mike Pettine as a senior defensive assistant.

Parker and Pettine worked together previously when the two were with the Green Bay Packers in 2019.

Jones made sure to say these decisions are not to say that Parker is overwhelmed by the responsibilities, but are a way to help find answers on the defensive side of the ball.

This is the second straight season the Cowboys will move their defensive coordinator from the field to the coaches' booth. Matt Eberflus made the move last season heading into Week 15.

Eberflus, like Parker, was in his first year in the role. At the time, the Cowboys ranked 31st in points allowed, were giving up 30 points per game, and were 29th in yards allowed per game at 374.9 yards. They ended up losing two out those final three games, allowing an average of 30 points per game.

The Cowboys fired Eberflus following the season.

Stationed in England this week, the Jaguars are adding a defensive back to their 53-man roster.

According to NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport, Jacksonville is signing Kaevon Merriweather off its practice squad to the active roster.

Merriweather appeared in Sunday’s win over the Eagles, playing 44 percent of special teams snaps and 34 percent of defensive snaps. He had one total tackle in the contest.

Last season, he appeared in 12 games for Tampa Bay and one game for Houston.

item.title: Getting Defensive: Week 6 fantasy plays led by Vikings, Steelers; top streaming defenses
item.description: Gary Davenport breaks down the fantasy football defense landscape headed into Week 6 of the 2026 NFL season.
item.content:encoded:
Back in the 1960s and 1970s, NFL offenses were terrorized by “The Purple People Eaters,” a defensive front in Minnesota littered with Pro Bowlers and anchored by a pair of Hall of Famers in Alan Page and Carl Eller. That defense helped propel the Vikings to a quartet of Super Bowls.

Now, no one is comparing the 2026 iteration of the Vikings defense to those all-time squads. But five weeks into the season, Minnesota is one of three undefeated teams remaining—and that defense is the reason why.

After holding the Saints to just 142 total yards and 13 points last week in New Orleans, the Vikings are currently third in total defense, third against the pass, fifth against the run and lead the league in scoring defense at just 12.8 points per game.

As good as those numbers are, it’s Brian Flores’ aggressiveness as defensive coordinator that is giving fantasy managers the vapors. In an NFL where no other team is blitzing at a 48 percent clip, Flores is sending an extra pass-rusher over 72 percent of the time. I know I’ve mentioned this before, but that is a staggering number—and it’s working.

Five games in, the Vikings are tied for the third-most sacks in the league with 17. They are one of three NFL teams with double-digit takeaways. And the Vikings are leading all defenses in fantasy points.

They may not be The Purple People Eaters.

But they have become an every-week must-start in fantasy leagues.

Fantasy Football Waiver Wire Week 6: Woody Marks and Germie Bernard step up
Germie Bernard and Woody Marks were thrust into larger roles than expected in Week 5. Both players will be asked to step up in Week 6, making them two of the best waiver wire adds this week.
  • Kyle Dvorchak,

THE NO-DOUBTERS

Minnesota Vikings (vs. Indianapolis Colts)

What? You thought I was finished? Never mind all that grape gushing I just did—if the Vikings were even a middling fantasy defense they would be making an appearance in this week’s column. The scheme Minnesota is playing is a nightmare for a team like the Colts than can’t take the top off opposing defenses. With no real threat of being burned over the top, the Vikings are going to stuff the box, blitz like crazy, smother the run game and then tee off on Daniel Jones, who has looked about as agile as a sloth on Valium.

Pittsburgh Steelers (at Tampa Bay Buccaneers)

In news that should surprise very few people, the Steelers are once again a top-five fantasy defense in 2026. But last week’s effort against the Indianapolis Colts was the team’s worst of the season—a single Cameron Heyward sack and no takeaways. T.J. Watt and the Steelers will get back on track this week in Tampa—last week’s win in Dallas aside, the last time rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels faced an actual NFL defense he struggled mightily, and no team has given up more fantasy points per game to defenses this year than the Buccaneers.

Jacksonville Jaguars (vs. Houston Texans—London)

No, the Jaguars aren’t moving across The Pond—at least not yet. But for the second week in a row, the AFC’s highest scoring fantasy defense will “host” a team in London, this time their AFC South rivals. This isn’t about the matchup—the Texans actually rank in the bottom-10 in fantasy points per game allowed to defenses. This about an excellent Jaguars defense that won’t have its routine disrupted this week. Jacksonville may be the AFC’s best team—and their balance is a big reason why.

San Francisco 49ers (vs. Washington Commanders)

If you know how the San Francisco 49ers are still undefeated despite a never-ending onslaught of injuries, explain it to me like I’m five. Despite being down their best edge-rusher in Seattle, the Niners sacked Sam Darnold five times, turned the Seahawks over four times and scored a defensive touchdown. At home? In primetime? Against the floundering Commanders. Top-five numbers. Book it. Wait, being that confident makes me nervous. You know what? Never mind. Double-book it.

Kansas City Chiefs (vs. Los Angeles Chargers)

From all indications, the Chiefs are back, and they come out of their bye week with a healthy Patrick Mahomes and a defense that ranks seventh in the league in points allowed. Across the AFC West in Los Angeles, the Chargers have completely imploded—the winless Bolts have no offensive identity, a rattled and beaten quarterback and an offense that is 25th in yards per game, 30th in points per game and second in fantasy points per game surrendered to opposing defenses. Heads roll in L.A. after the Chiefs roll at Arrowhead.

Seattle Seahawks (at Denver Broncos)

The bad news is that the Seahawks have to travel on a short week after a devastating loss to the 49ers at home to face a dangerous Denver Broncos team. But Seattle’s “Dark Side” defense has been consistently productive outside whatever the heck happened in Washington, including three sacks and three takeaways last week against San Francisco. The Broncos are having all kinds of trouble running the ball, and if they are forced to be one-dimensional Bo Nix had best wear comfortable shoes.

Fantasy Football Kicker Streamers: The 3 best pickups for Week 6
Cairo Santos is among the waiver wire options in a good spot headed into Week 6.
  • Denny Carter,

STREAMERS OF THE WORLD, UNITE!

Baltimore Ravens (at Cleveland Browns)

The Ravens may be 4-1, but the revamped defense bears just enough similarities to last year’s squad to make Baltimore fans uneasy. Still, that defense was OK in Atlanta last week with three sacks and a pick, and it should be far easier sledding in Week 6. Cleveland’s run game is among the NFL’s worst when Quinshon Judkins is healthy, and Cleveland quarterback Deshaun Watson was dropped eight times a week ago by the dominant pass rush (snicker) of the New York Jets.

Los Angeles Rams (vs. Arizona Cardinals)

Whatever tiny flecks of shine were left on one of the summer’s highest-drafted defenses were surgically removed by Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills on Monday night—you’d think we’d learn about “Dream Team” situations, and yet we do not even a little because people. But at 2-3 after a truly brutal schedule to start the season, the Rams finally get a break against a Cardinals team that just got smoked at home by the Lions. The Rams need this win—badly. And the Cardinals will pay the price.

New England Patriots (vs. New York Jets)

In the words of Samuel Clemens, it appears that reports of the demise of the New England Patriots have been exaggerated. The Patriots are quietly fifth in the league in yards allowed and fourth in the league in points allowed. Outside a huge outing at home against the Steelers that hasn’t really equated to fantasy points though, which has knocked them into streamer territory—a good place to be ahead of a Week 6 home date with a Jets team that has struggled mightily with offensive consistency this season.

New York Giants (vs. New Orleans Saints)

The Giants are quietly eighth in fantasy points among defenses after five weeks, despite being average in most statistical categories. There hasn’t been one massive week, one OK one and three duds, either—the Giants somehow find a way to at least get fantasy managers something, including five sacks in another bizarre game in D.C. (What is up in that stadium? Inter-dimensional vortex?). Add in a top-10 fantasy matchup for the position with the reeling Saints, and you have the definition of a matchup start.

Indianapolis Colts (vs. Tennessee Titans)

This is one of those “my defense is on bye and every other team in my league has two” type of plays—the Colts just got cooked on the road by the offensive juggernaut that is the Pittsburgh Steelers and have recorded negative fantasy points in two of five games this year in some scoring systems. But the Colts are at home facing a Tennessee Titans offense that is truly offensive—the Titans are the only team in the NFL averaging less than 250 yards of offense and 12 points per game.

Gary Davenport is a two-time Fantasy Sports Writers Association Football Writer of the Year. Follow Gary on X at @IDPGodfather.

item.title: NFL Panic Meter: Seahawks already showing more cracks than they did last season
item.description: The Seahawks' encore from their Super Bowl season is not off to a hot start.
item.content:encoded:
Last season, the Seattle Seahawks lost their Week 1 game. They went 17-2 the rest of the way.

This season, they've lost as many games by mid-October as they did in the final five months of last season.

It's not the end of the world to be 3-2, but there are more issues than you'd like to see. There are definitely more than we saw last season when Seattle steamrolled to a Super Bowl win.

The Seahawks' running game without Kenneth Walker III is an issue. Seattle was a run-first team that played impeccable defense on its way to a Super Bowl last season. That's hard to pull off when you're 30th in EPA (expected points added) per rushing play. The decision to move on from Walker when he was a free agent looks awful. Walker is a star for the Chiefs early this season and the Seahawks are getting nothing from their ground game. Maybe Zach Charbonnet can help turn things around when he returns, but he is coming off a torn ACL and was never a star in the offense.

That puts more pressure on the passing game and there are issues there too. Riding Jaxon Smith-Njigba worked great last season, but it's a big challenge to have an effective passing game with just one viable option. Smith-Njigba has 50 targets and noother Seahawk has more than 20. Smith-Njigba has 583 yards while nobody else is over 129. Smith-Njigba's 37 catches are more than Seattle's second, third and fourth top receivers combined. The rest of the wide receivers have 24 receptions total. JSN is a great player and that formula worked great last season, but it's hard to maintain.

When there's no running game and a narrow passing tree, it can put more on the plate of a turnover-prone quarterback. Sam Darnold has come a long way and has shed the bust label forever now that he helped guide a Super Bowl champion, but he still will turn it over too much. Darnold has five interceptions already despite missing almost two full games due to injury. The defense is still elite, but it's not great to be put in bad situations by the offense.

Seattle is still one of the NFL's elite teams. Losing to the 5-0 49ers isn't a terrible result, even at home. But it already looks tougher for them than it did for the entirety of last season.

Panic meter: Some alarms going off, but we'll trust coach Mike Macdonald to figure things out.

Can the Rams overcome awful special teams?

Bad special teams might have cost the Rams a Super Bowl last season. The special teams made huge mistakes in the final two losses to the Seahawks, including the NFC championship game.

And it's happening again.

The Rams had a field goal blocked in overtime on Monday, allowing the Bills to steal a win. They also missed a field goal in regulation. Rams coach Sean McVay was obviously bothered with his special teams after the game.

"Offensively and defensively we battled. Thought some of the coverage units, we did some really good stuff," McVay said. "Then in the kicking game, especially with our PAT/field goal, not close to good enough. It cost us the game."

But it's not new. The Rams were bad on special teams last season and did little to fix it. Their special teams are 32nd in DVOA. Even if the Rams make a change at kicker it doesn't change everything. This is going to be a problem McVay has to work around all season because he and the front office didn't bother to address it sufficiently in the offseason.

Panic meter: It's hard to be an elite team when you can't trust special teams to not blow games, and that's a big issue for the Rams going forward.

How will Commanders react to horrible tie?

It's fair to wonder how Sunday's end-of-game meltdown will affect the Commanders going forward. Coach Dan Quinn was asked if he worried the management mess in the final minute would cause players to lose confidence in him or the staff, and it's a fair question. Quinn said he didn't think it would.

"I know how tough our team is, the resilience, the toughness," Quinn said, via John Keim of ESPN. "They're able to handle adversity. We've got to get our execution nailed down. We have to be the team that we're capable of being. And that was the message that was loud and clear today."

The Commanders aren't out of anything at 1-3-1 in a bad NFC East. But it will be interesting to track if Sunday's debacle carries over.

Panic meter: The finish of Sunday's game was so horrifically awful, it wouldn't be a surprise if we look back on it as the moment the Commanders' season unraveled.

Is Christian Parker in trouble?

Jerry Jones said it was too early to consider removing Parker as the Dallas Cowboys' defensive coordinator. Then he hired a coach with 10 years of experience as either a defensive coordinator or head coach in the NFL.

The Cowboys announced that Mike Pettine was added to the staff as a senior defensive assistant. Had that move happened in the offseason, it would have looked like a smart move to support a 34-year-old coach who was a defensive coordinator for the first time. The move happening now, with the Cowboys struggling badly on defense, could be seen as a threat. It's also curious that Parker is heading up to the press box for play-calling, according to Cowboys owner Jerry Jones. They're searching for answers to a bad defense, and none of it can make Parker feel safe.

But Parker and Pettine have a history. Parker was an assistant for the Packers for two seasons while Pettine was defensive coordinator there. Parker tried to talk Pettine out of retirement when he was hired by the Cowboys, but Pettine said no, though there was a standing invitation for him to visit the Cowboys at their practice facility, according to an ESPN report in February. Still, having a longtime defensive coordinator on staff when the Cowboys are 31st in yards allowed and the owner is already being asked if he's considering replacing the current coordinator is a combustible mix.

Panic meter: Pettine isn't coming for Parker's job, but the speculation will be relentless until Dallas' defense turns it around.

How can Justin Herbert survive the season?

The Chargers' offensive line situation is as bad as it gets. The five starters on Sunday were four rookies, none of whom was a first-round pick, and veteran guard Cole Strange, who ranks near the bottom of Pro Football Focus' grades this season.

It's a horrible flashback to last season, when Herbert was the most pressured quarterback in the NFL behind a makeshift line. He was sacked five times Sunday. There's plenty more to come. Herbert has not played well this season, but with Rashawn Slater on injured reserve and Joe Alt dealing with a neck injury, it's going to get worse.

Panic meter: The Chargers can't protect their most valuable asset, which is a major problem. Again.

Can Michael Penix Jr. stay healthy?

The Atlanta Falcons are a different team with Penix in the lineup. We saw that in his three games back since he returned from ACL surgery. But then late in Sunday's game there was another injury.

Penix suffered a rib injury on a hard hit, and it was bad enough that Tua Tagovailoa had to take over in overtime. Tagovailoa threw an interception on his second pass of overtime, which showed again how bad the Falcons are without Penix. Penix's injury history is long, dating back to college and including three ACL tears.

Penix could return as soon as Week 6. But there is a growing question if the Falcons can rely on Penix to stay in the lineup, not just for the rest of this season but for when they consider whether to extend his contract.

Panic meter: It had to be disheartening for the Falcons to see Penix dealing with another injury, knowing that part of his story isn't going away.

item.title: Will Cowboys be buyers or sellers at the November 10 NFL trade deadline?
item.description: Should the Cowboys be buyers at the trade deadline?
item.content:encoded:
With the NFC East completely wide open, don’t be surprised if Jerry Jones is looking to make another big move to improve the Dallas Cowboys chances of winning the division. He is a known gambler and sitting on his hands and letting things play out is simply not his style. He’s more of a “damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead” type of person, and that attitude could come in to play with the November 10 NFL trade deadline approaching.

Between now and the trade deadline the Cowboys have four games to play against the Green Bay Packers, Philadelphia Eagles, Arizona Cardinals, and the Indianapolis Colts. Depending on how those games turn out, especially against the Eagles, could determine whether they are buyers like they have been this year or sellers to help reload for next year and beyond.

Today, we’ll at both sides of the argument.

Buyers

Jerry Jones has shown little hesitancy parting with future draft capital this year. He already traded for Rashan Gary, Dee Winters, Broderick Jones, and most recently Joey Porter Jr. As a result, they currently only have a total of four picks in the 2026 NFL Draft, one in the first, second, fourth, and seventh rounds. Despite that, Jerry Jones insists he’s more than willing to sacrifice the future to upgrade the present.

If true, the Cowboys could very well be buyers once again. Maxx Crosby continues to be rumored as a trade target for them, and fellow pass rusher Josh Sweat is another name thrown around, especially after the way the Cardinal season is circling the drain. To acquire either one of them via trade would likely take at least Dallas’ first-round pick next year with some change thrown in, further depleting next year’s draft capital.

It’s certainly not out of the realm of possibility, but may be unwise considering how the Cowboys are currently struggling defensively and not playing up to their talent on the offensive side of the ball.

Yes, it may result in a playoff berth, but another early exit without the tools to rebuild for the future could hurt the organization for a number of years. It would be another risk for Jerry Jones among many since purchasing the team.

Sellers

Depending on how the next four games play out for the Cowboys, it may make sense for them to start selling off their best trade assets to the highest bidder. Next year’s draft class is a talented one, especially at positions of “need” for Dallas. They are a team that has been building through the draft for a number of years now and stocking up on more draft capital could be in the best interest for the future of the organization.

The Cowboys have a number of trade assets who could be appealing to other teams around the league. George Pickens of course is at the top of the list. He could net them some high-round draft capital, but the limitations, because of the franchise tag, on signing a new contract with a new team hurts that value some. T.J. Bass could have some serious suitors as well, among others Dallas could be willing to part ways with.

Being sellers ahead of the November 10 trade deadline this year makes a lot of sense based on how things are playing out for the Cowboys so far this season. Right now there is no reason to believe this team can make waves in the playoffs. It may actually make more sense to reload and try again next year.

That, of course, depends on how Jerry Jones and Company view things. He may be more optimistic things can still be turned around. The game at the Packers on Sunday will be telling.

What do you think? Will the Cowboys be buyers or sellers at the trade deadline?

item.title: 3 Reasons Why the Chicago Bears Lost vs. the Packers
item.description: Not many things went right for Chicago on their trip to Green Bay. @BryanOrenchuk discusses his top 3 reasons why the Bears lost.
item.content:encoded:
We are on to the fifth installment of my new series for the 2026 season, where I recap what I believe were the three reasons the Chicago Bears won or lost the previous game.

In week 5 at Lambeau Field, we all know what happened. The question is why? Here are my three reasons.

1. Pass Defense

Not only did Packers QB Jordan Love have more time to throw in this game than he has in any game this season, but he also had a plethora of wide open options to choose from downfield. The pass rush had arguably their worst game of the season at the same time the secondary decided to have it’s worst game of the season. Not a good combination. Love completed 25 of 31 passes (81%) for 367 yards and 2 scores and was only sacked twice. Both at the end of the first half when GB was clearly trying to pass the ball to get some more points on the board before the break. This is the first game where the Bears secondary’s flaws were on full display for the world to see. Not having Coby Bryant alongside rookie Dillon Thieneman hurts. But with Jaylon Johnson looking washed and not one defensive back making plays in this one, GB carved up the Bears. Hopefully Kyler Gordon’s return will help boost the back end, but it is not looking good.

2. Turnovers

Bagent simply looked out of his league in this one. Not sure if it was the nerves of the rivalry, a great defensive scheme or what, but he was slow to process the field and made poor decisions when it was time to pull the trigger. We knew coming into this season that the offense would have to carry the defense, despite some early season success from Dennis Allen’s unit. After all, Chicago has enough weapons to keep up with anyone on offense. If the QB can get them the ball and keep the chains moving enough to put points on the board. That said, I absolutely could have give Bagent his own section here, but it was the turnovers, on the road against a humming Packers Offense that really hurt Chicago’s chances. We have seen Ben Johnson lead us to 4th quarter comebacks often, but it is becoming increasingly clear that is truly a Caleb Williams stat – and his ball security is critical to any success the offense experiences.

3. Kyle Monangai, RB

You have to wonder if Coach Johnson learned anything from last weeks contest when he fed the second year back a whopping 30 carries despite the teams RB1 healthy and on the sideline ready to play. Sure, Swift’s fumbles were back-breaking and Monangai had the hot hand, but 30 carries are a lot. Especially for a 5’8”, 207lb human. And Monangai ultimately got so banged up that he was held out of the first clash against Green Bay this season. Well, his absence was felt. Roschon Johnson, Monangai’s backup, is better served on special teams as he makes next to zero impact for the offense. And while Swift held his own, the one-two punch of him and Monangai was sorely missed as the latter provides the juice that the team needs with his rugged and assertive playstyle. Hopefully he is back on Christmas Day, along with Caleb Williams, because that offense simply doesn’t look the same without those two.

What about you? Who or what stood out the most in the loss to the Cheese?

item.title: Jerry Jones on Dak Prescott's postgame interaction with driver: Fans can express themselves
item.description: Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott wasn't happy about hearing from a driver after last Thursday's loss to the Buccaneers, but the interaction didn't bother Cowboys owner Jerry Jones.
item.content:encoded:
Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott wasn't happy about hearing from a driver after last Thursday's loss to the Buccaneers, but the interaction didn't bother Cowboys owner Jerry Jones.

The driver said "embarrassing" as Prescott walked by him in an AT&T Stadium tunnel and Prescott replied by sarcastically calling the driver, who does not work for the team, a "tough guy" before adding "get his ass out of here." During an appearance on 105.3 The Fan, Jones said he's fine with people speaking their mind.

“I didn’t pay a lot of attention to it. It doesn’t impact me at all," Jones said. "The driver in question was not an employee. Fans can express themselves and and should express themselves. Whether he was our employee or not, he was a fan it sounds like. So, I'm for our fans expressing themselves."

The rest of Jones's radio appearance focused on what the Cowboys can do on the field to make future expressions from the fanbase a little more positive.

item.title: What is the 49ers plan at receiver without Deebo Samuel?
item.description: The Niners have 3 receivers on their practice squad.
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers lost another piece of their offensive core when Deebo Samuel went down with a hamstring injury against the Seattle Seahawks in Week 5. Samuel, 30, had been looking to hit the edge before pulling up and fumbling on a non-contact play.

He’ll now miss a few weeks, only adding to the injury bug that San Francisco is facing at receiver. The 49ers have now lost Ricky Pearsall, De’Zhaun Stribling, Christian Kirk, Demarcus Robinson, Samuel, and Khadarel Hodge all to injuries for some period of time.

The 49ers trotted out Brandin Cooks for the first time, while Jacob Cowing played a heavy number of snaps behind Mike Evans. Additionally, we saw Jordan Watkins get 22 snaps as well. Right now, those three are the team’s top depth after Evans, who is still recovering in his own right from a painful rib injury.

What is the 49ers plan at receiver without Samuel?

“Well, yeah, with Deebo out, we have five guys on the roster and Deebo being out, that would be four,“ head coach Kyle Shanahan said about his receivers. So the next guys up to get activated would be one of the three guys on practice squad. Because also in that game Jake went down with an ankle. He ended up being all right, but the numbers got low real quick. That’s why we always like to get five up for game day. We’ve got four guys on our roster, so we’ll most likely decide on one of those guys throughout the week.”

Currently, the 49ers have three receivers on their practice squad: Wesley Grimes, Will Pauling, and Xavier Smith. So will they look for more reinforcements during the week? Shanahan doesn’t believe so, at least for now.

“I think we have enough,” Shanahan added. “We’ve got three guys on practice squad also who can help. Anytime you lose this number of guys, four guys or five guys whatever it is, it’s a huge challenge. But, we do have guys in this building who can do it and we’ll always look.”

The 49ers, and other teams in the NFL, usually have five or six receivers, with one potentially being inactive on game day. San Francisco doesn’t even have the five healthy bodies on their 53-man roster, let alone a sixth.

So, until players come back, it could be a significant dose of Mike Evans, as it was on Sunday when he had seven catches for 113 yards and a touchdown. The 49ers face the Washington Commanders and Atlanta Falcons over the next two weeks before their bye, giving them a chance to start 7-0 as the league’s best team.

But for that to happen, they’ll have to figure something more out at receiver, as they’ve really struggled to get much production out of the position the last few weeks.

item.title: Fantasy Football: Chase Brown leads a group of young, highly-touted RBs (and one WR) that it's time to panic over
item.description: The fantasy football Panic Meter is in full effect for these players ahead of Week 6.
item.content:encoded:
Five weeks into the NFL season, it's time to take a hard look at some big-name fantasy football players who aren't living up to expectations. Let's get into my Week 6 Panic Meter and see who's giving us real reasons to worry.

Chase Brown, Cincinnati Bengals: SOME PANIC

I have some panic about Chase Brown, and it's not necessarily because of his workload. It's because I'm watching these games and wondering how much longer Cincinnati can continue giving him the same opportunities if he isn't going to make more happen with them.

Through five games, Brown has 71 carries for 246 yards, averaging just 3.5 yards per attempt. That's a significant drop from the 4.4 yards per carry he averaged last season. He's still getting opportunities, but the production on the ground hasn't been good enough.

If you watched the game this past Sunday, Samaje Perine looked noticeably better between the tackles. He finished with 68 rushing yards and caught a touchdown pass while Brown managed just 39 rushing yards. That's concerning when you consider how much of Brown's fantasy value depends on maintaining a substantial role in this offense.

Now, I'm not suggesting Perine is about to take over the backfield. Brown has 24 receptions through five games, and I still expect him to command the larger receiving role.

But what happens if Perine continues to earn meaningful opportunities?

If we're keeping it real, Brown hasn't been particularly good as a runner. If Perine starts taking away rushing attempts, short-yardage opportunities and some of the receiving work that helps keep Brown's fantasy production afloat, we're looking at a much different situation than we anticipated. Honestly, is it that far-fetched of a story? I don't think so. 

The passing game has been his safety net. I don't want to see that safety net getting smaller.

I'm not selling Brown at a discount because his overall involvement remains encouraging. But the efficiency concerns are legitimate, and Perine has done enough to make this a conversation worth having.

Cam Skattebo, New York Giants: SOME PANIC

Cam Skattebo is another player who I'm starting to get a little uncomfortable with what we're seeing. Let's start with the production. He's averaging 3.6 yards per carry, has just one rushing touchdown and has already fumbled four times through five games. Only one of those fumbles has been lost, but four fumbles this early in the season is not something we can completely dismiss.

Especially when the rushing production isn't exactly making up for it.

Now, the positive is that Skattebo still accounts for the majority of New York's rushing attempts. He's carried the ball 81 times, representing approximately 55% of the Giants' team rushing attempts. The opportunities are there, and he's still clearly the leader of this backfield.

But here's where my concern really starts.

Coming out of Arizona State, we knew Skattebo could catch the football. And during his rookie season, we saw just how valuable he could be as a receiving option in fantasy. He wasn't simply a running back who could catch a screen. He was somebody who could legitimately contribute through the passing game.

That hasn't translated the same way this season.

With Jameis Winston running this offense, we're not seeing the same commitment to getting Skattebo involved underneath. He has just 10 receptions through five games. For a player struggling to generate efficiency on the ground, those missing receiving opportunities are significant.

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Basketball league for the 2026-27 NBA season

And let's not ignore the overall environment. The Giants have just one rushing touchdown as a team. Skattebo owns it, but that's not exactly encouraging when you're trying to project weekly fantasy upside.

I still believe in Skattebo's ability, and I don't think his role is in immediate danger. But between the fumbles, the inefficient rushing attack and the lack of receiving production, there are enough issues here to warrant concern.

Ashton Jeanty, Las Vegas Raiders: TOTAL PANIC

I'm moving Ashton Jeanty into Total Panic, and it's primarily because of what I'm seeing when I watch him play. He doesn't look healthy.

This isn't the Jeanty we watched dominate at Boise State. It's not even the Jeanty we saw during his rookie season. Right now, he looks like a running back who's banged up, struggling to create explosive plays and having a difficult time making defenders miss.

The frustrating part is that the opportunity hasn't disappeared.

Jeanty has 88 carries for 291 yards and 22 receptions for another 215 yards. He's still getting the lion's share of the backfield work, but he's averaging just 3.3 yards per carry and hasn't scored a rushing touchdown.

Even the receiving game, which has helped salvage his fantasy production, hasn't been particularly clean. We've seen dropped passes and missed opportunities from a player who should be one of the most dependable offensive weapons on this roster. And now, we have legitimate injury concerns.

At some point, we have to wonder whether continuing to play through these injuries is helping anybody. Could the Raiders eventually decide to give Jeanty some time off to get healthy? I'm not suggesting that's their plan, but watching him struggle to look like himself week after week makes it a legitimate question.

I'm not panicking about his talent. I'm panicking about his health and whether we're going to see the version of Jeanty we drafted anytime soon.

Jeremiyah Love, Arizona Cardinals: TOTAL PANIC

I think Jeremiyah Love is going to be a really good NFL running back.

I also think it's ok to talk about what we're actually getting from him in fantasy right now. Because the expectations and the production aren't remotely aligned.

Love was supposed to arrive in Arizona and immediately become one of the most dynamic offensive playmakers in football. We've seen flashes of that ability, especially during his Week 3 performance against San Francisco. But flashes don't win fantasy matchups.

Through five games, Love has 245 rushing yards, 36 receiving yards and two total touchdowns. He's averaging just 3.7 yards per carry, and over his past two games, he's managed only 85 rushing yards. Meanwhile, Arizona is 1-4, has just traded Marvin Harrison Jr. and looks like an organization searching for answers.

Tyler Allgeier continues to command meaningful opportunities. He has 35 carries and 12 receptions compared to Love's 67 carries and 11 receptions. For a player we expected to dominate this backfield, that's not exactly what fantasy managers signed up for.

And remember, Love recently described this as the longest year of his life. We're only five games into his rookie season. Whether it's the physical adjustment to the NFL, the offensive environment or simply the frustration of losing, none of it is particularly encouraging.

Here's what makes this difficult. We've seen how explosive Love can be. You don't want to bench a player with that kind of ability because one play could completely change his fantasy day.

But how confident are you actually putting him in your lineup? Right now, Love feels much closer to a lower-end RB2 than the difference-making fantasy running back many of us expected. I'm not giving up on the player. I'm giving up on the idea that his preseason expectations are realistic in this current environment.

Jaylen Waddle, Denver Broncos: TOTAL PANIC

I don't know how else to describe what's happening in Denver other than saying this offense looks broken. And Jaylen Waddle is one of the biggest fantasy casualties.

Outside of one explosive performance, Waddle has been incredibly disappointing. He has 18 receptions for 204 yards and one touchdown through five games. The problem? Eight catches and 138 of those yards came in one game against Jacksonville. Take that game away and Waddle has 10 receptions for 66 yards across four games. Four games!

That's nowhere close to the production we expected from someone with his talent. But I don't think this is entirely a Waddle problem. Bo Nix hasn't played well. Davis Webb struggled as the offensive play-caller through the first four weeks. Sean Payton took those responsibilities back in Week 5, and the results weren't much better. Waddle finished with two catches for 19 yards against the Chargers.

What makes this even more frustrating is that Denver has an offensive line capable of supporting a productive offense. Yet, this passing attack continues to struggle with consistency, efficiency and creating meaningful opportunities for its playmakers. Nix is completing fewer than 60% of his passes and averaging just 5.8 yards per attempt. That's simply not a recipe for supporting reliable weekly fantasy receivers.

And while Waddle deserves his share of the criticism, I have a difficult time placing the majority of the blame on him. We've seen what he can do when the offense gets him involved. That Jacksonville performance wasn't an accident. The problem is that we haven't seen anything close to that production consistently.

At this point, I'm in Total Panic on Waddle as an every-week fantasy starter. Frankly, I'm concerned about just about every significant fantasy option in this Denver offense, including Nix. Maybe Payton eventually gets things figured out. Maybe the offense finds its rhythm. But I'm done assuming the turnaround is coming simply because the talent is there.

item.title: 5 takeaways from Bills instant classic win over Rams
item.description: The adrenaline has not left my body
item.content:encoded:
I’m working on a few hours of sleep, and I’m actually surprised I was able to fall asleep in the wee hours of Tuesday morning given the mixture of cortisol and adrenaline that were coursing through my veins after the Buffalo Bills 37-34 win over the Rams on Monday Night Football in Week 5.

This game had nine lead changes, six-consecutive touchdown drives to end regulation, and was capped with the first overtime victory of Josh Allen’s NFL career to date.

Josh Allen reminded everyone who the NFL’s best player is

On April 21, 2026, I sent the following tweet, because I realized despite feeling this way for years, I had never actually put it on the Twitter/X record. And nothing is official until that happens right?

As you can see, that tweet went decently viral… plenty of Bills fans liked it, agreed, etc. Plenty of Ravens/Chiefs fans felt differently.

A few months later, I wrote my rationale here at Rumblings.

And I’m not a victory lap person. I know how much of a rollercoaster the NFL season is. Keenly aware.

BUT MY LORD JOSH ALLEN SURE AS HELL VALIDATED THAT TWEET LAST NIGHT.

OK, that is all. Onto the next point.

Jim Leonhard’s defense is currently not Jim Leonhard’s defense

I’m not going to pretend I know/understand all the calls and concepts in Leonhard’s defensive scheme. But as an avid college football fan, I vividly remember those Wisconsin defenses. They blitzed from everywhere. You just never knew from where. Their secondaries were outstanding despite lacking five-star recruits.

They lived in man. They dropped defensive tackles into underneath throwing lanes. Confused the hell out of quarterbacks.

And I think these two tweets that resurfaced last night from Anthony Prohaska of Cover 1 that were sent in the offseason tell essentially the whole story right now on the defensive side of the ball for the Bills:

Couldn’t have written it better myself, Anthony. Whether it’s because Leonhard doesn’t trust his secondary loaded with youth and newcomers to Buffalo, or they’re simply still learning all of the intricacies of it, the Bills secondary is a major problem entering Week 6. No question about it.

I do happen to think the more reps this secondary gets together, the better it’ll become. And the more they’ll understand what Leonhard is asking of them. I’m also of the belief more youngsters should see the field in the back seven — like Kaleb Elarms-Orr and Jalon Kilgore.

And for as much as I initially want to write that Leonhard might be meddling/micro-managing too much… again, Buffalo’s defense, in its current state schematically, does not resemble the Wisconsin defenses he coordinated with great aplomb and perennial success.

Joe Brady is learning too…

I didn’t hate the Bills wasting time for the end of the first half before trying to move the ball. I did not like the timeout after they let the clock bleed inside 40 seconds.

If you’re going to take that route — milk the clock so you’re legitimately with the ball last before halftime — you can’t then stop the clock yourself because you can’t get into the right play.

Unequivocally a mistake. Brady owned it postgame. Maybe could’ve used a timeout on the final defensive drive of regulation too right? When it seemed like the defense was gassed. However, Brady doesn’t operate in a vacuum as the NFL’s sole head coach. Sean McVay, a head coach since 2017, didn’t exactly ace his game-management test before sending out Harrison Mevis in overtime last night. And things could be worse on this front… ask Commanders fans.

Yes, the Bills probably should’ve tush pushed Allen twice to get the clock inside two minutes in overtime.

But you know what? Even if that was technically the smarter thing to do, and I’m all for attempting to make the most prudent decision at all times, the tush-push plan to “waste time” in case of a miss would’ve been focusing too much on the worst-case scenario occurring and attempting not to lose. And I’m glad, for a change, the Bills coach was concerned with one thing… winning.

…but his game plan was masterful

The Bills were down their two best outside separators at receiver for this game. That cannot be overstated in its importance. We’ve seen many offenses, even early in 2026, completely crumble without their No. 1 wideout.

So the Bills pounded the rock. Utilized two perfectly executed running back screens. Called an exquisite — and legal — pick play on the Keon Coleman touchdown. Schemed open a two-point conversion! And let Allen be Allen as a runner.

Now, of course, Brady didn’t necessarily plan for Allen to run it 10 times for 121 yards. But Brady understood those vertical routes were going to draw defenders out of the intermediate level of the field to give his quarterback ample room to morph into an agigtated moose with And 1 mixtape agility in space.

The Bills (passing) offense went into this game with one hand tied behind its back, and Brady’s game plan helped Buffalo escape with a win.

Lastly, he clearly very much understands if the Bills are to go to where they intend to this season, James Cook will be an integral facet of this team. Brady going right back to Cook after his overtime fumble will go a long way with the running back himself and the rest of this Bills team.

The Bills are 4-1

That’s a takeaway? Yes it is. Caught up in all the defensive turmoil and Cook fumbles, I think it’s an incredibly obvious yet important reminder. Of course, the defensive woes and Cook putting the ball on the ground isn’t sustainable. Those areas of the team must improve.

At this stage, as the Bills are clearly far from a finished product, they’d much rather be 4-1 with clear flaws then 3-2, 2-3, or 1-4 while having played cleaner, more balanced football.
